# Purpose of this analysis

In this example, we use weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) to identify co-expressed gene modules [@Langfelder2008]. 
WGCNA uses a series of correlations to identify sets of genes that are expressed together in your data set. 
This is a fairly intuitive approach to gene network analysis which can aid in interpretation of microarray & RNA-seq data. 

As output, WGCNA gives groups of co-expressed genes as well as an eigengene x sample matrix (where the values for each eigengene represent the summarized expression for a group of co-expressed genes) [@Langfelder2007]. 
This eigengene x sample data can, in many instances, be used as you would the original gene expression values. 
In this example, we use eigengene x sample data to identify differentially expressed modules between our treatment and control group

This method does require some computing power, but can still be run locally (on your own computer) for most refine.bio datasets.
As with many clustering and network methods, there are some parameters that may need tweaking.

# Identifying co-expression gene modules with WGCNA - RNA-seq

## Install libraries

See our Getting Started page with [instructions for package installation](https://alexslemonade.github.io/refinebio-examples/01-getting-started/getting-started.html#what-you-need-to-install) for a list of the other software you will need, as well as more tips and resources.

We will be using `DESeq2` to normalize and transform our RNA-seq data before running WGCNA, so we will need to install that [@Love2014].

Of course, we will need the `WGCNA` package [@Langfelder2008].
But `WGCNA` also requires a package called `impute` that it sometimes has trouble installing so we recommend installing that first [@Hastie2020]. 

For plotting purposes will be creating a `sina` plot and heatmaps which we will need a `ggplot2` companion package for, called `ggforce` as well as the `ComplexHeatmap` package [@Gu2020].  

```{r}
if (!("DESeq2" %in% installed.packages())) {
  # Install this package if it isn't installed yet
  BiocManager::install("DESeq2", update = FALSE)
}

if (!("impute" %in% installed.packages())) {
  # Install this package if it isn't installed yet
  BiocManager::install("impute")
}

if (!("WGCNA" %in% installed.packages())) {
  # Install this package if it isn't installed yet
  install.packages("WGCNA")
}

if (!("ggforce" %in% installed.packages())) {
  # Install this package if it isn't installed yet
  install.packages("ggforce")
}

if (!("ComplexHeatmap" %in% installed.packages())) {
  # Install this package if it isn't installed yet
  install.packages("ComplexHeatmap")
}

#install.packages("languageserver") #For VSCode r extension
```

## Determine parameters for WGCNA

To identify which genes are in the same modules, WGCNA first creates a weighted network to define which genes are near each other. 
The measure of "adjacency" it uses is based on the correlation matrix, but requires the definition of a threshold value, which in turn depends on a "power" parameter that defines the exponent used when transforming the correlation values. 
The choice of power parameter will affect the number of modules identified, and the WGCNA modules provides the  `pickSoftThreshold()` function to help identify good choices for this parameter. 

# Run with only roots normalized counts
```{r}
sft <- pickSoftThreshold(normalized_counts_roots,
  dataIsExpr = TRUE,
  corFnc = cor,
  networkType = "signed"
)
```
This `sft` object has a lot of information, we will want to plot some of it to figure out what our `power` soft-threshold should be. 
We have to first calculate a measure of the model fit, the signed $R^2$, and make that a new variable. 

```{r}
sft_df <- data.frame(sft$fitIndices) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(model_fit = -sign(slope) * SFT.R.sq)
```

Now, let's plot the model fitting by the `power` soft threshold so we can decide on a soft-threshold for power. 

```{r}
sft_plot <- ggplot(sft_df, aes(x = Power, y = model_fit, label = Power)) +
  # Plot the points
  geom_point() +
  # We'll put the Power labels slightly above the data points
  geom_text(nudge_y = 0.1) +
  # We will plot what WGCNA recommends as an R^2 cutoff
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, col = "red") +
  # Just in case our values are low, we want to make sure we can still see the 0.80 level
  ylim(c(min(sft_df$model_fit), 1.05)) +
  # We can add more sensible labels for our axis
  xlab("Soft Threshold (power)") +
  ylab("Scale Free Topology Model Fit, signed R^2") +
  ggtitle("Scale independence") +
  # This adds some nicer aesthetics to our plot
  theme_classic()

sft_plot 


#output_file <- file.path(fig_dir, "sft_plot.pdf")
#ggsave(plot = sft_plot , output_file, dpi = 600, units = "in", height = 4, width = 6) 

```

Using this plot we can decide on a power parameter. 
WGCNA's authors recommend using a `power` that has an signed $R^2$ above `0.80`, otherwise they warn your results may be too noisy to be meaningful. 

If you have multiple power values with signed $R^2$ above `0.80`, then picking the one at an inflection point, in other words where the $R^2$ values seem to have reached their saturation [@Zhang2005].
You want to a `power` that gives you a big enough $R^2$ but is not excessively large.

So using the plot above, going with a power soft-threshold of `14`!

If you find you have all very low $R^2$ values this may be because there are too many genes with low expression values that are cluttering up the calculations. 
You can try returning to [gene filtering step](#define-a-minimum-counts-cutoff) and choosing a more stringent cutoff (you'll then need to re-run the transformation and subsequent steps to remake this plot to see if that helped). 

## Run WGCNA!

We will use the `blockwiseModules()` function to find gene co-expression modules in WGCNA, using `14` for the `power` argument like we determined above. 

This next step takes some time to run.
The `blockwise` part of the `blockwiseModules()` function name refers to that these calculations will be done on chunks of your data at a time to help with conserving computing resources.

Here we are using the default `maxBlockSize`, 5000 but, you may want to adjust the `maxBlockSize` argument depending on your computer's memory.
The authors of WGCNA recommend running [the largest block your computer can handle](https://peterlangfelder.com/2018/11/25/blockwise-network-analysis-of-large-data/) and they provide some approximations as to GB of memory of a laptop and what `maxBlockSize` it should be able to handle:

> • If the reader has access to a large workstation with more than 4 GB of memory, the parameter maxBlockSize
can be increased. A 16GB workstation should handle up to 20000 probes; a 32GB workstation should handle
perhaps 30000. A 4GB standard desktop or a laptop may handle up to 8000-10000 probes, depending on
operating system and other running programs.

[@Langfelder2016]

```{r}
dim(normalized_counts_roots) # To see how many genes we have. 22883, I will use this as maxBlockSize, so I have all genes in one block
```

```{r}
bwnet <- blockwiseModules(normalized_counts_roots,
  maxBlockSize = 22883, # What size chunks (how many genes) the calculations should be run in
  TOMType = "signed", # topological overlap matrix
  power = 14, # soft threshold for network construction
  numericLabels = TRUE, # Let's use numbers instead of colors for module labels
  randomSeed = 1234, # there's some randomness associated with this calculation
  # so we should set a seed
)
```

## Module identification using mergeCutH 0.25
https://bioinformaticsworkbook.org/tutorials/wgcna.html#gsc.tab=0
```{r}
picked_power = 14
temp_cor <- cor       
cor <- WGCNA::cor         # Force it to use WGCNA cor function (fix a namespace conflict issue)
netwk <- blockwiseModules(normalized_counts_roots,                # <= input here
                          maxBlockSize = 22883, # What size chunks (how many genes) the calculations should be run in

                          # == Adjacency Function ==
                          power = picked_power,                # <= power here
                          networkType = "signed",

                          # == Tree and Block Options ==
                          deepSplit = 2,
                          pamRespectsDendro = F,
                          # detectCutHeight = 0.75,
                          minModuleSize = 30,
                          maxBlockSize = 4000,

                          # == Module Adjustments ==
                          reassignThreshold = 0,
                          mergeCutHeight = 0.25,

                          # == TOM == Archive the run results in TOM file (saves time)
                          saveTOMs = T,
                          saveTOMFileBase = "ER",

                          # == Output Options
                          numericLabels = T,
                          randomSeed = 1234,
                          verbose = 3)
```



Let's take a look at the modules WGCNA identified.
```{r}
plot(bwnet$dendrograms[[1]])

# Convert labels to colors for plotting
mergedColors = labels2colors(bwnet$colors)
# Plot the dendrogram and the module colors underneath
# Start the graphics device
#png(paste0(fig_dir, "dendro_allgenes.png"), res = 600, height = 4, width = 6, units = "in")
pdf(file = file.path(fig_dir, "dendro_allgenes.pdf"), width = 6, height = 4)

# Create the plot
dendro_allgenes <- plotDendroAndColors(
  bwnet$dendrograms[[1]],
  mergedColors[bwnet$blockGenes[[1]]],
  "Module colors",
  dendroLabels = FALSE,
  hang = 0.03,
  addGuide = TRUE,
  guideHang = 0.05 )

# Close the graphics device
dev.off()

```


The `TOMtype` argument specifies what kind of topological overlap matrix (TOM) should be used to make gene modules.
You can safely assume for most situations a `signed` network represents what you want -- we want WGCNA to pay attention to directionality. 
However if you suspect you may benefit from an `unsigned` network, where positive/negative is ignored see [this article](https://peterlangfelder.com/2018/11/25/signed-or-unsigned-which-network-type-is-preferable/) to help you figure that out [@Langfelder2018].

There are a lot of other settings you can tweak -- look at `?blockwiseModules` help page as well as the [WGCNA tutorial](https://horvath.genetics.ucla.edu/html/CoexpressionNetwork/Rpackages/WGCNA/Tutorials/) [@Langfelder2016].



## Explore our WGCNA results

The `bwnet`  object has many parts, storing a lot of information. 
We can pull out the parts we are most interested in and may want to use use for plotting. 

In `bwnet` we have a data frame of eigengene module data for each sample in the `MEs` slot. 
These represent the collapsed, combined, and normalized expression of the genes that make up each module. 

```{r}
module_eigengenes <- bwnet$MEs

# Print out a preview
head(module_eigengenes)
```

## Heatmap of module eigengenes
```{r}

#z-score
cal_z_score <- function(x){
  (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
}
MEs0_roots_tnorm <- t(apply(MEs0_roots_t, 1, cal_z_score))

library(pheatmap)
library(RColorBrewer)

mod_all_heatmap_zscore <- pheatmap(MEs0_roots_tnorm,
         color = myColor3,
         breaks = myBreaks,
         cluster_rows = TRUE,
         cluster_cols = T,
         # add row gap
         row_gap = 4,
         border_color = "black",
         #main = "Module eigengenes",
         annotation_col = sampledataord_roots_ann,
         #annotation_row = metadata_roots_ann,
         annotation_colors = sampledataord_roots_ann_colors,
         gaps_col = gap_geno,
         show_colnames = F,
         show_rownames = T)
mod_all_heatmap_zscore
ggsave(plot = mod_all_heatmap_zscore, paste0(fig_dir, "heatmapZscore_module_allroots.pdf"), dpi = 600, units = "in", height = 8, width = 8)
```

## Module QC 

Modified from: https://github.com/cxli233/SimpleTidy_GeneCoEx#reorder-rows-and-columns

### Summary statistics for each module and condition and look at their expression pattern using mean
```{r} 
head(MEs0_roots) #Module eigengenes
#Add independent columns for tissue, day and genotype
ME_sampledata <- MEs0_roots %>%
  mutate(
    Tissue = sampledataord_roots$Tissue,
    Day = sampledataord_roots$Day,
    Genotype = sampledataord_roots$Genotype
  )
head(ME_sampledata)

ME_sampledata_long <- ME_sampledata %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("ME"), names_to = "Module", values_to = "Eigenvalue")

head(ME_sampledata_long)

#save the environment until now
#save.image(file = "3.NetworkAnalysis/4_RDGA_NetworkAnalysis.RData")
load("3.NetworkAnalysis/4_RDGA_NetworkAnalysis.RData")


#Mean eigenvalues for each module and condition
library(dplyr)
modules_mean_exp_long <- ME_sampledata_long %>% 
  dplyr::group_by(Module, Tissue, Day, Genotype) %>% 
  dplyr::summarise(mean_ME = mean(Eigenvalue)) %>% 
  ungroup()

head(modules_mean_exp_long)

# Save the mean eigenvalues for each module and condition
write.csv(modules_mean_exp_long, file = paste0(out_dir, "modules_mean_exp_long.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

#At which tissue, day and genotype is each module most highly expressed
module_peak_exp <- modules_mean_exp_long %>% 
  group_by(Module) %>% 
  slice_max(order_by = mean_ME, n = 1) 
  
module_peak_exp_ordered <- module_peak_exp %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  arrange(Tissue, Day, Genotype, desc(mean_ME))

module_peak_exp_ordered

module_peak_exp_tissueord <- module_peak_exp %>%
  mutate(Tissue = factor(Tissue, levels = tissues_ordered)) %>%  # set custom order
  arrange(Tissue, Day, Genotype, desc(mean_ME))
module_peak_exp_tissueord 


write.csv(module_peak_exp_ordered, file = paste0(out_dir, "module_peak_exp_ordered.csv"))
write.csv(module_peak_exp_tissueord, file = paste0(out_dir, "module_peak_exp_tissueord.csv"))

#Save with flextable
library(flextable)
module_peak_exp_ordered_flex <- flextable(module_peak_exp_ordered)
module_peak_exp_ordered_flex <- flextable(module_peak_exp_ordered) %>%
  set_table_properties(width = .5, layout = "autofit") %>%
  align(align = "center", part = "all") %>%
  set_header_labels(
    Tissue = "Tissue",
    Day = "Day",
    Genotype = "Genotype",
    Module = "Module",
    mean_ME = "Mean Eigenvalue"
  ) %>%
  set_caption("At which tissue, day and genotype is each module most highly expressed")

#Save to a file

  group_by(Module) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = mean_ME, n = 3)

# Save the top conditions for each module

# Top 3 lowest mean eigengene expressions per module
```

## Module eigengenes associated with groups
# Add the module assignment to the metadata 
Using linear modeling via limma on module eigengenes is a very good and statistically sound approach to:

Formally test which modules are associated with a condition (e.g., Day, Genotype, or Tissue),
Control for multiple testing, and
Quantify effect size and significance of associations.
```{r}
library(limma)
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)

head(MEs0_roots)
head(bwnet$MEs)

# 1. Make sure rownames of metadata match the rows of module eigengenes
# (MEs0_roots rows = samples)
all(rownames(MEs0_roots) == rownames(sampledataord_roots))  # Should be TRUE

# 2. Create design matrix for multi-factor model
design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + Tissue + Day + Genotype, data = sampledataord_roots)
colnames(design) <- make.names(colnames(design))  # Clean names for limma

# 3. Transpose eigengenes to genes (rows) × samples (columns)
ME_matrix <- t(MEs0_roots)  # Now rows are modules, columns are samples
# Remove non-numeric columns (like treatment, Tissue, Day, Genotype)
ME_matrix <- MEs0_roots %>%
  dplyr::select(starts_with("ME")) %>%
  as.matrix() %>%
  t()  # transpose to modules x samples


# 4. Fit linear model
fit <- lmFit(ME_matrix, design)

# 5. Define contrasts if needed (e.g., comparing day5 vs day2)
# Alternatively, skip this step if you want full coefficient outputs
# contrast.matrix <- makeContrasts(Day5vsDay2 = Dayday5 - Dayday2, levels = design)
# fit2 <- contrasts.fit(fit, contrast.matrix)

fit2 <- eBayes(fit)  # Use full model without contrast if you're testing all terms

# 6. Extract results per coefficient (e.g., GenotypeStampede, Dayday5, each Tissue)
results_list <- list()
for (coef_name in colnames(fit2$coefficients)) {
  top <- topTable(fit2, coef = coef_name, number = Inf) %>%
    rownames_to_column("Module") %>%
    mutate(Contrast = coef_name)
  results_list[[coef_name]] <- top
}

# 7. Combine all results
module_trait_lm_results <- bind_rows(results_list)

# 8. Save or inspect
head(module_trait_lm_results)
write.csv(module_trait_lm_results, file = paste0(out_dir, "module_trait_lm_results.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

```

## Modeling association with each condition combination (Sample_ID)
Test the association between each WGCNA module eigengene and the specific combination of Tissue, Genotype, and Day (your Sample_ID), then you should model Sample_ID as a single factor.

This allows you to treat each unique experimental condition as its own group
```{r}
# 1. Design matrix using Sample_ID as a factor
design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + Sample_ID, data = sampledataord_roots)
colnames(design) <- make.names(colnames(design))  # Clean names

# 2. Prepare eigengene matrix (modules × samples)
eigengene_matrix <- MEs0_roots %>%
  dplyr::select(starts_with("ME")) %>%
  as.matrix() %>%
  t()

# 3. Fit linear model with limma
library(limma)
fit <- lmFit(eigengene_matrix, design)
fit <- eBayes(fit)

# 4. Extract statistics for all Sample_IDs
results_list <- lapply(colnames(design), function(sample) {
  topTable(fit, coef = sample, number = Inf) %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("Module") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(Sample_ID = sample)
})
results_all <- dplyr::bind_rows(results_list)

# 5. View or save
head(results_all)

# 6. Save the results
write.csv(results_all, file = paste0(out_dir, "module_sampleid_lm_results.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

#Top condition per module

top_conditions_per_module <- results_all %>%
  group_by(Module) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = logFC, n = 3)  # or slice_min() for most negative

# Save the top conditions per module
write.csv(top_conditions_per_module, file = paste0(out_dir, "top_conditions_per_module_sampleid.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

## Specific module-condition associations
Compute z-scores of module eigengenes across conditions and identify highly specific module-condition associations, with emphasis on the 3 defined tissue clusters.
```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Use your existing ME_sampledata_long
# Columns: Module, Tissue, Day, Genotype, Eigenvalue

# 1. Z-score calculation across modules
ME_zscore <- ME_sampledata_long %>%
  group_by(Module) %>%
  mutate(zscore = scale(Eigenvalue)) %>%
  ungroup()

# 2. Define tissue clusters
cluster1_tissues <- c("Hypocotyl", "RootCrown")  # day 5 only
cluster2_tissues <- c("MatureBranchedZoneTaproot", "YoungBranchedZoneTaproot", "AUZTaproot", "AUZBasalRoots")
cluster3_tissues <- c("RootTipTaproot", "RootTipBasalRoots")
cluster4_tissues <- c("RootCrown")  # day 2 only

# 3. Assign Cluster based on tissue and day
ME_zscore <- ME_zscore %>%
  mutate(
    Cluster = case_when(
      Tissue %in% cluster1_tissues & Day == "day5" ~ "Cluster1",
      Tissue %in% cluster2_tissues ~ "Cluster2",
      Tissue %in% cluster3_tissues ~ "Cluster3",
      Tissue %in% cluster4_tissues & Day == "day2" ~ "Cluster4",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

# 4. Filter for strong condition-specific module expression
specific_modules <- ME_zscore %>%
  filter(abs(zscore) > 1.5)  # Adjust threshold if needed

# 5. Optional: save or inspect
write.csv(specific_modules, file = paste0(out_dir, "ME_zscore_gt1p5_cluster.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

```

```{r}
library(dplyr)

# Function to get modules passing all z-score thresholds within each group (tissue or cluster)
get_consistent_modules <- function(df, group_var, z_threshold) {
  df %>%
    group_by(Module, !!sym(group_var)) %>%
    summarise(all_above = all(zscore > z_threshold), .groups = "drop") %>%
    filter(all_above) %>%
    select(Module, !!sym(group_var)) %>%
    mutate(z_threshold = z_threshold)
}

# Set z-score thresholds
z_thresholds <- c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5)

# Initialize empty results
mod_tissue_filtered <- data.frame()
mod_cluster_filtered <- data.frame()

# Loop over thresholds to collect qualifying modules
for (z in z_thresholds) {
  # Filter by tissue
  temp_tissue <- get_consistent_modules(ME_zscore, "Tissue", z)
  mod_tissue_filtered <- bind_rows(mod_tissue_filtered, temp_tissue)

  # Filter by cluster
  temp_cluster <- get_consistent_modules(ME_zscore, "Cluster", z)
  mod_cluster_filtered <- bind_rows(mod_cluster_filtered, temp_cluster)
}

# Save the filtered results
write.csv(mod_tissue_filtered, file = paste0(out_dir, "ME_zscore_threshold_tissue.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(mod_cluster_filtered, file = paste0(out_dir,"ME_zscore_threshold_cluster.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

```

```{r}
library(dplyr)

# Step 1: Calculate z-scores for each module
ME_zscore <- ME_sampledata_long %>%
  group_by(Module) %>%
  mutate(zscore = scale(Eigenvalue)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Step 2: Define tissue groups for clusters
cluster1_tissues <- c("Hypocotyl", "RootCrown")
cluster2_tissues <- c("MatureBranchedZoneTaproot", "YoungBranchedZoneTaproot", "AUZTaproot", "AUZBasalRoots")
cluster3_tissues <- c("RootTipTaproot", "RootTipBasalRoots")
cluster4_tissues <- c("RootCrown")  # day2 only

# Step 3: Annotate clusters
ME_zscore <- ME_zscore %>%
  mutate(
    Cluster = case_when(
      Tissue %in% cluster1_tissues & Day == "day5" ~ "Cluster1",
      Tissue %in% cluster2_tissues & Genotype == "RedHawk" ~ "Cluster2_Rh",
      Tissue %in% cluster2_tissues & Genotype == "Stampede" ~ "Cluster2_St",
      Tissue %in% cluster3_tissues ~ "Cluster3",
      Tissue %in% cluster4_tissues & Day == "day2" ~ "Cluster4",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Cluster))  # remove unmatched

# Step 4: Function to filter modules based on z-score threshold and proportion of samples
filter_modules_by_cluster <- function(df, z_thresh = 1.5, min_prop = 0.6) {
  df %>%
    group_by(Module, Cluster) %>%
    summarise(
      n_total = n(),
      n_passing = sum(zscore > z_thresh),
      prop_passing = n_passing / n_total,
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    filter(prop_passing >= min_prop)
}

# Step 5: Apply filter for desired thresholds
modules_60 <- filter_modules_by_cluster(ME_zscore, z_thresh = 1, min_prop = 0.6)
modules_80 <- filter_modules_by_cluster(ME_zscore, z_thresh = 1, min_prop = 0.8)
modules_90 <- filter_modules_by_cluster(ME_zscore, z_thresh = 1, min_prop = 0.9)

# Step 6: Save or inspect
write.csv(modules_60, file = paste0(out_dir, "modules_clust2bygeno_z1_60perc.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(modules_80, file = paste0(out_dir, "modules_clust2bygeno_z1_80perc.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(modules_90, file = paste0(out_dir, "modules_clust2bygeno_z1_90perc.csv"), row.names = FALSE)


```

## Hub genes for each module 
Create separate objects for each module, using a for loop and the assign() function to dynamically create variable names.

This code will create separate genes_modX, expr_modX, TOM_modX, and edge_list_modX objects for each module in modules_of_interest, where X is the module number.

## 1. For loop to create expression, genes and TOM objects for each module

```{r}
library(WGCNA)
library(tidyr)

# Enable parallel processing
enableWGCNAThreads()

# Check the number of threads WGCNA will use
library(parallel)
nThreads <- detectCores()
print(paste("WGCNA will use", nThreads, "threads."))

# Enable parallel processing with a specific number of cores
enableWGCNAThreads(nThreads = 6)
```

```{r}
#modules numbers and number of genes by module
table(module_df$colors)
#order modules 0 to 27
sorted_mod <- sort(unique(module_df$colors))
sorted_mod
modules_of_interest = sorted_mod[1] # All modules as numbers. Run 1st module separately, then run all modules, because it's the largest and takes longer and module 0 are the genes that don't belong to any cluster.
modules_of_interest = sorted_mod[2:28] #
picked_power = 14

for (module in modules_of_interest) {
  genes_of_interest = module_df %>%
    subset(colors == module)

  assign(paste0("genes_mod", module), genes_of_interest)

  expr_of_interest = normalized_counts_roots_t[genes_of_interest$gene_id,]

  assign(paste0("expr_mod", module), expr_of_interest)

  # Only recalculate TOM for modules of interest
  TOM = TOMsimilarityFromExpr(t(expr_of_interest),
                              power = picked_power)

  # Add gene names to row and columns
  row.names(TOM) = row.names(expr_of_interest)
  colnames(TOM) = row.names(expr_of_interest)

  assign(paste0("TOM_mod", module), TOM)

  edge_list = data.frame(TOM) %>%
    mutate(
      gene1 = row.names(.)
    ) %>%
    pivot_longer(-gene1) %>%
    dplyr::rename(gene2 = name, correlation = value) %>%
    unique() %>%
    subset(!(gene1==gene2)) %>%
    mutate(
      module1 = module_df[gene1,]$colors,
      module2 = module_df[gene2,]$colors
    )

  assign(paste0("edge_list_mod", module), edge_list)
  
  # Export edge_list file to be read into Cytoscape, VisANT, etc
  write_delim(edge_list,
              file = paste0(out_dir,"module_edgelist/edgelist_mod", module, ".tsv"),
              delim = "\t")
}
```


## 2. For loop to get the hub genes for each module 
```{r}
# List of modules
modules_of_interest = sorted_mod[2:28]

nTop = 30 #number of top hub genes

# Loop over each module
for (module in modules_of_interest) {
  expr_of_interest = get(paste0("expr_mod", module))
  genes_of_interest = get(paste0("genes_mod", module))

  genenames = row.names(expr_of_interest)
  expr_of_interest_t = t(expr_of_interest)

  IMconn = softConnectivity(expr_of_interest_t[,genenames])

  top = (rank(-IMconn) <= nTop)

  # Subset the TOM to the top genes
  TOM = get(paste0("TOM_mod", module))
  TOMhub = TOM[top, top]

  hub_list = data.frame(TOMhub) %>%
    mutate(
      gene1 = row.names(.)
    ) %>%
    pivot_longer(-gene1) %>%
    dplyr::rename(gene2 = name, correlation = value) %>%
    unique() %>%
    subset(!(gene1==gene2)) %>%
    mutate(
      module1 = module_df[gene1,]$colors,
      module2 = module_df[gene2,]$colors
    )

  # Assign the objects to dynamically named variables
  assign(paste0("genes_of_interest_mod", module), genes_of_interest)
  assign(paste0("TOMhub_mod", module), TOMhub)
  assign(paste0("hub_list_mod", module), hub_list)

  #write hub list to a .csv
  write.csv(hub_list, file = paste0(out_dir,"hubgenes_mod/hub_list_mod", module, ".csv"))
}

#write objects TOMhub_modX to csv
for (module in modules_of_interest) {
  TOMhub = get(paste0("TOMhub_mod", module))
  write.csv(TOMhub, file = paste0(out_dir, "hubgenes_mod/TOMhub_mod", module, ".csv"))
}
```

```{r}
#Add significance testing between genotypes for each gene × tissue × day

library(rstatix)


library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(rstatix)
library(purrr)

# Safe t-test to avoid crashing on constant data
safe_t_test <- purrr::possibly(.f = rstatix::t_test, otherwise = tibble(p = NA_real_))

sig_results <- allmod_df %>%
  dplyr::filter(gene_id %in% suberin_gene_df_unique$gene_id) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(suberin_gene_df_unique, by = "gene_id", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  dplyr::filter(
    (Day == "day5" & Tissue %in% ordered_tissues) |
    (Day == "day2" & Tissue %in% day2_tissues)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(gene_name, Tissue, Day) %>%
  tidyr::nest() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(test = map(data, ~ safe_t_test(.x, value ~ Genotype))) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(test) %>%
  rstatix::add_significance("p") %>%   # Use raw p for significance labeling
  dplyr::select(gene_name, Tissue, Day, p, p.signif)



suberin_expr_summary_sig <- suberin_expr_summary %>%
  dplyr::left_join(sig_results, by = c("gene_name", "Tissue", "Day"))

#save the significance results
write.csv(suberin_expr_summary_sig, file = paste0(out_dir, "suberin_expr_summary_sig.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
  CASP1    = "Phvul.007G152900, Phvul.007G153000",
  MYB36    = "Phvul.003G148200",
  PER64    = "Phvul.001G003800",
  SCR      = "Phvul.008G077000",
  SHR      = "Phvul.002G010700, Phvul.003G235000, Phvul.003G236300",

) %>%

# Step 2: Join with expression data and summarize replicates

  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(gene_name, Tissue, Genotype, Day) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(mean_expr = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    Tissue = factor(Tissue, levels = ordered_tissues),
    gene_name = factor(gene_name, levels = rev(names(marker_pv_gene_ids)))
  )
```
